title: Create and organize a GameObject
summary: Create an empty or primitive GameObject, name it clearly, and place it in the Hierarchy.
example_questions: How do I create an object?
Where do I add a new GameObject?
How can I organize objects in the Hierarchy?
Create an empty parent object
prerequisites: A Unity scene is open
steps: In the Hierarchy, right-click an empty area.
Choose Create Empty, or choose a primitive from the 3D Object or 2D Object submenu.
Rename the new object to describe its role.
Use the Transform component to set its position, rotation, and scale.
verification: Confirm the object appears in both the Hierarchy and Scene view.
Select it and verify that its Transform appears in the Inspector.
common_mistakes: Editing an object while Play Mode is active and losing the change afterward.
Leaving many objects with generic names such as GameObject or Cube.

title: Add a component to a GameObject
summary: Use the Inspector to add behaviour such as physics, rendering, audio, or scripts to the selected object.
example_questions: How do I add a component?
Where is Add Component?
How do I attach behaviour to an object?
Put a script on my player
prerequisites: A GameObject exists in the active scene
steps: Select the target GameObject in the Hierarchy.
At the bottom of its Inspector, click Add Component.
Search for the component by name and select it.
Configure the new component's exposed fields.
verification: Confirm the component is listed on the selected object's Inspector.
common_mistakes: Adding the component to the wrong selected object.
Searching for a script that still has compilation errors.

title: Create and assign a material
summary: Create a Material asset, select a compatible shader, and assign it to a renderer.
example_questions: How do I change an object's color?
How do I put a material on a cube?
Assign a texture to an object
Why is my object pink?
prerequisites: A rendered 3D object exists
The active render pipeline is known
steps: In the Project window, right-click inside an Assets folder and choose Create > Material.
Name the material and choose a shader compatible with the project's render pipeline.
Set its base color and optional texture.
Drag the material onto the object in the Scene view or into its renderer's Materials list.
verification: Confirm the object's appearance changes in the Scene and Game views.
common_mistakes: Using a Built-in shader in URP or HDRP, which can produce a pink material.
Changing a shared material when an object-specific copy was intended.

title: Make a 3D object respond to physics
summary: Add a Rigidbody and an appropriate 3D Collider so an object can fall and collide.
example_questions: How do I make an object fall?
How do I enable physics?
Make my cube react to gravity
My object passes through the floor
prerequisites: The moving object and floor exist in a 3D scene
steps: Select the moving object and add a Rigidbody component.
Add a suitable 3D Collider if the object does not already have one.
Ensure the floor has a 3D Collider.
Enter Play Mode and observe the object.
verification: The object falls due to gravity and stops on the floor.
common_mistakes: Mixing Rigidbody2D or Collider2D with 3D physics components.
Enabling Is Kinematic while expecting gravity to move the object.
Moving a Rigidbody by changing Transform every frame.

title: Make a 2D object respond to physics
summary: Add Rigidbody2D and Collider2D components to participate in Unity's separate 2D physics system.
example_questions: How do I add 2D physics?
Make my sprite fall
My 2D player passes through platforms
Rigidbody2D setup
prerequisites: A Sprite or other 2D GameObject exists
steps: Select the moving 2D object and add Rigidbody2D.
Add an appropriate Collider2D to the moving object.
Ensure platforms have Collider2D components.
Enter Play Mode to test the interaction.
verification: The object responds to 2D gravity and collides with the platform.
common_mistakes: Mixing 2D and 3D physics components.
Using a trigger collider when a solid collision was intended.

title: Respond to a collision in a script
summary: Use the correct 2D or 3D collision callback on a MonoBehaviour attached to a participating object.
example_questions: How do I detect a collision?
Run code when objects touch
How does OnTriggerEnter work?
My collision function is not called
prerequisites: The relevant physics components are already configured
steps: Decide whether the interaction should be a physical collision or a trigger.
Attach a MonoBehaviour script to one participating object.
For 3D, implement OnCollisionEnter or OnTriggerEnter; for 2D, use the callback ending in 2D.
Log the other object's name first to verify the callback before adding gameplay logic.
verification: The Console prints once when the objects first interact.
common_mistakes: Using a 3D callback with 2D components.
Spelling or capitalizing Unity message methods incorrectly.
Having no Rigidbody on either participating object.

title: Create basic player movement
summary: Read player input, calculate a direction, and move through the appropriate physics component.
example_questions: How do I move my player?
Control a character with WASD
Basic movement script
Make the character respond to keyboard input
prerequisites: A player GameObject exists
The project input system has been chosen
steps: Choose whether the project uses the Input System package or the legacy Input Manager.
Read a two-axis movement value in a player-control script.
Normalize or clamp the direction so diagonal movement is not faster.
Apply movement through Rigidbody, Rigidbody2D, or CharacterController rather than mixing several movement systems.
verification: The player moves in every intended direction at a consistent speed.
common_mistakes: Multiplying physics movement by frame time in the wrong place.
Changing Transform directly on a dynamic Rigidbody.
Using code for a different input backend than the project setting.

title: Make a camera follow the player
summary: Configure a simple scripted follow camera or a Cinemachine camera with a player target.
example_questions: How do I make the camera follow the player?
My character walks away from the camera
Set up a third-person camera
How do I use Cinemachine follow?
prerequisites: A player object and Main Camera exist
steps: Decide between a simple fixed-offset camera and Cinemachine.
For Cinemachine, install or enable the package and create an appropriate Cinemachine camera.
Assign the player Transform to the camera's Tracking Target or Follow field.
Adjust position, damping, and framing while testing in Play Mode.
verification: Move the player and confirm that the camera maintains the intended framing.
common_mistakes: Assigning the visual child instead of the stable player root.
Having multiple enabled AudioListeners or competing active cameras.

title: Create and reuse a prefab
summary: Turn a configured scene object into a reusable Prefab asset and understand instances and overrides.
example_questions: How do I create a prefab?
Reuse the same enemy many times
What is a prefab instance?
Save a GameObject as an asset
prerequisites: A configured GameObject exists in the scene
steps: Create a Prefabs folder in Assets if one does not exist.
Drag the configured GameObject from the Hierarchy into that folder.
Create additional instances by dragging the Prefab asset into the scene.
Use the Overrides menu deliberately when applying or reverting instance changes.
verification: Edit the Prefab asset and confirm that its non-overridden instances update.
common_mistakes: Applying an unwanted scene-specific value to every instance.
Unpacking a prefab without needing to break its connection.

title: Play an animation with an Animator Controller
summary: Connect animation clips through an Animator Controller and use parameters to change states.
example_questions: How do I play an animation?
Set up an Animator Controller
Switch from idle to walk
My animation clip does not play
prerequisites: At least one compatible animation clip exists
steps: Create an Animator Controller asset.
Assign it to the target object's Animator component.
Open the Animator window and drag animation clips into it as states.
Create parameters and transitions for state changes, then update those parameters from gameplay code.
verification: Enter Play Mode and watch the active state highlight in the Animator window.
common_mistakes: Leaving the Animator without a controller.
Creating a transition whose conditions can never become true.
Using clips configured for an incompatible avatar type.

title: Create a UI button that performs an action
summary: Add a Canvas and Button, then connect its On Click event to a public component method.
example_questions: How do I make a button?
Run a function when UI is clicked
Create a start button
My Unity button does nothing
prerequisites: A scene is open
steps: Create a Button through GameObject > UI; Unity also creates a Canvas and EventSystem when needed.
Select the Button and find its On Click event in the Inspector.
Add a listener, drag in the GameObject containing the target script, and select a compatible public method.
Enter Play Mode and click the button.
verification: The configured method runs exactly once when the button is clicked.
common_mistakes: Dragging the script asset instead of the scene GameObject containing the component.
Testing clicks outside Play Mode.
Missing or disabled EventSystem.

title: Change from one scene to another
summary: Add scenes to the build configuration and load them through SceneManager.
example_questions: How do I load another scene?
Change levels when a button is clicked
Go from menu to game
SceneManager setup
prerequisites: The source and destination scenes have been saved
steps: Add the destination scene to the project's build scene list or build profile.
Import UnityEngine.SceneManagement in the controlling script.
Call SceneManager.LoadScene with the intended scene name or build index.
Trigger that method from gameplay or a UI event.
verification: Enter Play Mode, trigger the transition, and confirm the destination scene loads.
common_mistakes: Misspelling a scene name.
Forgetting to include the scene in the build configuration.
Expecting ordinary scene objects to persist without DontDestroyOnLoad.

title: Play sound from a GameObject
summary: Use an AudioSource with an AudioClip and make sure the scene has exactly one active AudioListener.
example_questions: How do I play a sound?
Add background music
Play an effect when jumping
Why is there no audio?
prerequisites: An imported AudioClip exists
steps: Select the sound-producing GameObject and add an AudioSource.
Assign the AudioClip and configure volume, looping, and spatial blend.
Use Play On Awake for automatic playback or call Play/PlayOneShot from a script.
Confirm that an enabled AudioListener exists, normally on the Main Camera.
verification: Enter Play Mode and hear the clip under the intended condition.
common_mistakes: Having zero or multiple active AudioListeners.
Using full 3D spatial blend while the listener is too far away.
Muting the Game view audio toggle.

title: Set up basic lighting in a 3D scene
summary: Use directional, point, or spot lights and inspect exposure, shadows, and environment settings.
example_questions: Why is my scene dark?
How do I add lights?
Set up sunlight
My shadows look wrong
prerequisites: A rendered 3D scene exists
steps: Add or select a Directional Light for broad outdoor illumination.
Rotate it to choose the direction of light and shadows.
Adjust intensity and shadow settings for the current render pipeline.
Inspect the Environment Lighting and exposure settings if the entire scene remains too dark or bright.
verification: Objects are readable in both Scene and Game views and shadows point consistently.
common_mistakes: Changing Scene-view lighting while judging a different Game camera result.
Using extreme intensity to compensate for incorrect exposure.

title: Make an agent navigate with a NavMesh
summary: Prepare walkable geometry, build navigation data, and assign a destination to a NavMeshAgent.
example_questions: How do I make an enemy walk to the player?
Set up NavMesh
My NavMeshAgent does not move
Add pathfinding
prerequisites: Walkable level geometry exists
AI Navigation is available
steps: Install or enable the AI Navigation package if required by the Unity version.
Add a NavMeshSurface to an appropriate level object and configure what it collects.
Build the NavMesh and verify the walkable visualization.
Add NavMeshAgent to the moving character and set a reachable destination from a script.
verification: The agent follows the baked walkable area to the destination.
common_mistakes: Placing the agent away from the built NavMesh.
Using a destination outside all reachable areas.
Building navigation data before the level geometry is ready.

title: Create and attach a C# MonoBehaviour script
summary: Create a C# script, keep the class and filename aligned, and attach it to a GameObject.
example_questions: How do I create a script?
Attach C# code to an object
What are Start and Update?
My script cannot be added
prerequisites: Unity's configured code editor is available
steps: In the Project window, right-click an Assets folder and create a MonoBehaviour/C# script.
Give it a valid descriptive class name and open it in the code editor.
Use Start for initialization and Update only for work that must be checked each rendered frame.
Save the file, wait for Unity to compile, and attach it to the intended GameObject.
verification: The script appears as a component without a Missing or compilation warning.
common_mistakes: Renaming the class without matching the filename.
Trying to attach a script while any project compilation error exists.
Putting expensive work in Update unnecessarily.

title: Create a playable build
summary: Select a platform, include the correct scenes, configure player settings, and build outside the Assets folder.
example_questions: How do I export my game?
Make a Windows build
Create an executable
Which scenes are included in the build?
prerequisites: At least one saved scene is ready to run
steps: Open Build Profiles or Build Settings, depending on the Unity version.
Choose the target platform and switch to it if necessary.
Add and order every required scene, placing the startup scene first.
Review Player Settings, then build into a dedicated folder outside Assets.
verification: Launch the produced build and test scene transitions, input, audio, and quitting.
common_mistakes: Building inside the Assets folder.
Leaving the startup scene out of the build configuration.
Assuming behaviour in the Editor guarantees identical build behaviour.

title: Parent objects and understand local transforms
summary: Build a hierarchy where child objects follow a parent while keeping local and world coordinates clear.
example_questions: How do I make one object follow another?
What is a parent GameObject?
Why did my child object move?
What is local position versus world position?
prerequisites: Two GameObjects exist in the scene
steps: Drag the intended child onto the intended parent in the Hierarchy.
Expand the parent and select the child.
Edit the child's local Position, Rotation, and Scale relative to its parent.
Move the parent and confirm the child follows as part of the hierarchy.
verification: Moving or rotating the parent also moves the child while preserving the child's local offset.
common_mistakes: Parenting to the wrong similarly named object.
Confusing local coordinates in the Inspector with world coordinates.
Using a scaled parent and unintentionally scaling every child.

title: Use tags and layers correctly
summary: Use tags to identify object roles and layers to control rendering, raycasts, and physics interactions.
example_questions: What is the difference between tags and layers?
How do I tag my player?
How can a camera ignore objects?
How do I configure collision layers?
prerequisites: A GameObject exists in the scene
steps: Select the object and use the Tag dropdown for its gameplay identity, creating a tag if needed.
Use the Layer dropdown for filtering and interaction rules.
Configure the Physics or Physics 2D layer collision matrix when layers should not collide.
Use the same layer in camera culling masks or raycast masks where appropriate.
verification: CompareTag recognizes the object and the configured camera, physics, or raycast filter includes or excludes it.
common_mistakes: Using object names as permanent identity.
Creating a layer when a tag was intended.
Changing only a child layer when the whole hierarchy should change.

title: Set up controls with the Input System
summary: Create an Input Actions asset, define actions and bindings, and connect them to player code.
example_questions: How do I use Unity's new Input System?
Set up keyboard and controller controls
How do I create an input action?
Why does PlayerInput not call my method?
prerequisites: The Input System package is installed
steps: Create an Input Actions asset in the Project window.
Add an action map and actions such as Move, Jump, and Pause.
Add bindings for the intended keyboard, mouse, or gamepad controls and save the asset.
Use PlayerInput or generated C# callbacks to read the action values in a player script.
verification: Open the Input Debugger or log callbacks and confirm each configured device triggers the expected action.
common_mistakes: Mixing old Input Manager code with an Input System-only project setting.
Forgetting to save changes in the Input Actions editor.
Using mismatched callback names or action maps.

title: Select a 3D object with a mouse raycast
summary: Convert the pointer position into a camera ray and detect a collider with Physics.Raycast.
example_questions: How do I click a 3D object?
Cast a ray from the mouse
Select an object in the Game view
Why does my raycast miss the object?
prerequisites: An active camera and a target with a 3D Collider exist
steps: Detect the pointer click with the project's selected input backend.
Create a ray using the gameplay camera and the current pointer screen position.
Call Physics.Raycast with an appropriate maximum distance and optional layer mask.
Use the returned RaycastHit collider or transform to identify the clicked target.
verification: Log the hit object's name and click several targets and empty space.
common_mistakes: The target has no Collider.
Using a Scene-view camera assumption instead of the gameplay Camera.
Using Physics2D.Raycast for 3D colliders or Physics.Raycast for 2D colliders.

title: Spawn and remove GameObjects at runtime
summary: Instantiate prefab instances with a chosen transform and destroy them when their lifetime ends.
example_questions: How do I spawn an enemy?
Create a bullet from a prefab
How do I destroy an object?
Instantiate something at a spawn point
prerequisites: A prefab and a MonoBehaviour that will spawn it exist
steps: Expose a prefab reference and assign it in the Inspector.
Choose or create a Transform to act as the spawn point.
Call Instantiate with the prefab, position, and rotation when the spawn condition occurs.
Call Destroy on the instance when it is no longer needed, optionally with a short delay.
verification: Enter Play Mode and confirm each trigger creates one correctly positioned instance that is later removed.
common_mistakes: Assigning a scene instance instead of the prefab asset.
Spawning every frame without a cooldown.
Destroying the prefab reference rather than the created instance.

title: Delay work with a coroutine
summary: Use IEnumerator and yield instructions for readable time-based sequences without blocking Unity.
example_questions: How do I wait two seconds?
Make a timer in Unity
What is a coroutine?
Run actions in a timed sequence
prerequisites: A MonoBehaviour script is attached to an active GameObject
steps: Create a method returning IEnumerator.
Place each stage of the sequence around yield return statements such as new WaitForSeconds.
Start the sequence with StartCoroutine.
Keep a Coroutine reference or use a clear condition if the sequence may need to stop early.
verification: Log timestamps or observe the staged behavior and confirm the Editor stays responsive during the wait.
common_mistakes: Calling the IEnumerator method without StartCoroutine.
Creating a blocking loop on the main thread.
Expecting WaitForSeconds to ignore Time.timeScale.

title: Expose script settings in the Inspector
summary: Serialize private fields for editable settings while keeping implementation details encapsulated.
example_questions: How do I show a variable in the Inspector?
What does SerializeField do?
Why is my field not editable in Unity?
Should Unity variables be public?
prerequisites: A working MonoBehaviour script exists
steps: Declare the setting as a supported serializable field, usually private.
Add the SerializeField attribute above the field.
Optionally add Header, Tooltip, Range, or Min attributes to make editing safer.
Save, let Unity compile, then configure the value on each component instance or prefab.
verification: The field appears in the Inspector and its configured value is available when Play Mode starts.
common_mistakes: Expecting a C# property to serialize automatically.
Editing a runtime value and expecting it to persist after Play Mode.
Making every implementation field public only to expose it.

title: Reference objects and components from a script
summary: Assign references in the Inspector or find nearby components once, then validate them before use.
example_questions: How do I reference another GameObject?
How does GetComponent work?
Drag an object into a script field
Why is my component reference null?
prerequisites: The source script and target object or component exist
steps: Choose an Inspector-assigned field for a deliberate external dependency or GetComponent for a component on the same object.
Use a strongly typed field such as Rigidbody instead of a generic GameObject when possible.
Assign the field in the Inspector or cache GetComponent during Awake.
Validate required references and show a useful error rather than failing later.
verification: Select the component and confirm its field is assigned, then enter Play Mode without a missing-reference error.
common_mistakes: Calling expensive scene searches every frame.
Forgetting prefab instances need valid references too.
Assuming GetComponent searches unrelated objects.

title: Debug scripts with the Console
summary: Read the first compiler or runtime error, navigate to its source, and use focused log messages to inspect state.
example_questions: How do I fix a red Console error?
Where can I see Debug.Log?
Unity says scripts have compiler errors
How do I debug my code?
prerequisites: The Console window is available
steps: Open Window > General > Console and enable Error Pause only when useful.
Fix the first compiler error before later errors because one syntax problem can cause many messages.
Double-click the message to open the exact file and line.
Add focused Debug.Log messages with the relevant object as context, then remove noisy logs after diagnosis.
verification: The Console has no unexpected red errors and the diagnostic log shows the expected values and execution order.
common_mistakes: Starting with the last error instead of the first.
Ignoring the stack trace and object context.
Logging every frame until the useful message is buried.

title: Fix a NullReferenceException
summary: Use the stack trace to find which reference is missing and assign or initialize it at the correct lifecycle stage.
example_questions: What does NullReferenceException mean?
Why is my variable null?
Fix object reference not set
My script crashes on this line
prerequisites: A Console stack trace identifies the failing script and line
steps: Double-click the exception and inspect every reference used on the highlighted line.
Check whether an Inspector field is unassigned, GetComponent returned null, or initialization has not run yet.
Assign or initialize the dependency in the appropriate place, commonly the Inspector or Awake.
Add a validation check with a clear message when the reference is required.
verification: Repeat the original action and confirm the exception no longer appears and the intended behavior occurs.
common_mistakes: Adding a null check that hides a required missing dependency.
Fixing a scene instance but not the prefab.
Accessing another component before its initialization order is guaranteed.

title: Import and configure a 2D sprite
summary: Set an image to Sprite type, choose pixels per unit and filtering, and place it with a SpriteRenderer.
example_questions: How do I import a sprite?
Why is my pixel art blurry?
Put an image in a 2D scene
What does pixels per unit mean?
prerequisites: A supported image file has been copied into Assets
steps: Select the texture asset and set Texture Type to Sprite (2D and UI).
Choose Single or Multiple mode and set consistent Pixels Per Unit.
For pixel art, use Point filtering and disable inappropriate compression; otherwise keep suitable smooth filtering.
Apply the import settings and drag the sprite into the scene to create a SpriteRenderer.
verification: The sprite has the expected world size and appears sharp or smooth according to the chosen art style.
common_mistakes: Using inconsistent Pixels Per Unit across related art.
Forgetting to click Apply.
Using a UI Image when a world-space SpriteRenderer was intended.

title: Build a 2D level with a Tilemap
summary: Create a Grid and Tilemap, prepare a palette, paint tiles, and add collision where needed.
example_questions: How do I create a Tilemap?
Paint a 2D level
Add collision to tiles
How does the Tile Palette work?
prerequisites: 2D Tilemap Editor support is installed and tile sprites are imported
steps: Create a Rectangular Tilemap, which also creates a parent Grid.
Open the Tile Palette window and create a palette asset.
Drag sliced tile sprites into the palette and save the generated Tile assets.
Paint the Tilemap, then add TilemapCollider2D and optionally CompositeCollider2D for solid level geometry.
verification: Tiles align to the grid and a Rigidbody2D player collides with intended solid tiles.
common_mistakes: Painting on the wrong active Tilemap.
Using mismatched sprite sizes or Pixels Per Unit.
Adding 3D colliders to a 2D Tilemap.

title: Create responsive UI with Canvas anchors
summary: Choose the right Canvas mode and anchor UI elements so they adapt to different resolutions.
example_questions: Why does my UI move at another resolution?
How do Canvas anchors work?
Make responsive Unity UI
Set up a Canvas Scaler
prerequisites: A Canvas and at least one UI element exist
steps: Use Screen Space Overlay for a straightforward HUD unless the design needs a camera or world-space Canvas.
Set Canvas Scaler to Scale With Screen Size and choose a reference resolution.
Select each RectTransform and choose anchors matching the intended screen edge, corner, stretch, or center behavior.
Test several Game view aspect ratios and adjust offsets and layout groups.
verification: The UI remains readable and attached to its intended region at wide, tall, and reference resolutions.
common_mistakes: Positioning everything with fixed pixels and center anchors.
Scaling UI elements by Transform scale instead of RectTransform layout.
Testing only one Game view resolution.

title: Display text with TextMeshPro
summary: Add crisp UI text, import essential TMP resources, and update the displayed value from a script.
example_questions: How do I add text to the UI?
Display the player's score
Why is TMP text missing?
Change TextMeshPro text from a script
prerequisites: A Canvas exists for UI text
steps: Create UI > Text - TextMeshPro and import TMP Essential Resources if prompted.
Set the font asset, size, alignment, wrapping, and RectTransform.
Expose a TMP_Text or TextMeshProUGUI reference in the controlling script.
Assign it in the Inspector and set its text property when the displayed value changes.
verification: The text is sharp, fits its intended area, and updates when the underlying value changes.
common_mistakes: Forgetting to import TMP resources.
Updating the label every frame when the value rarely changes.
Leaving the RectTransform too small and clipping the text.

title: Create a UI health bar
summary: Represent current health with a Slider or filled Image and update it from one authoritative health component.
example_questions: How do I make a health bar?
Update a UI Slider from health
Create a player HUD
Make an Image fill as health changes
prerequisites: A Canvas and a script that owns current and maximum health exist
steps: Create a Slider with interaction disabled or an Image using Filled type.
Set the range to zero through maximum health, or normalize health to zero through one.
Reference the UI element from a presenter or health script.
Update the display whenever health changes and clamp the underlying value.
verification: Apply damage and healing and confirm the bar reaches empty and full at the correct values.
common_mistakes: Allowing UI code and gameplay code to own separate health values.
Dividing integers without converting to float for a normalized fill.
Leaving the decorative Slider interactable.

title: Control animation transitions with parameters
summary: Create Animator states and use parameters and transition conditions to switch cleanly between animations.
example_questions: How do I switch from idle to run?
Use Animator parameters
Why is my animation transition stuck?
Set an Animator trigger from code
prerequisites: An Animator Controller with at least two animation states exists
steps: Add a Bool, Float, Int, or Trigger parameter describing the gameplay state.
Create transitions between Animator states and add clear conditions.
Choose whether Has Exit Time should wait for the current clip or transition immediately.
Set the parameter from gameplay code using the exact parameter name or a cached hash.
verification: Watch the Animator during Play Mode and confirm the active state and parameter change under the intended condition.
common_mistakes: Leaving Has Exit Time enabled for a transition that must happen immediately.
Using a misspelled parameter name.
Creating transitions with contradictory conditions.

title: Create a simple particle effect
summary: Configure a Particle System's shape, lifetime, speed, color, and emission for a small visual effect.
example_questions: How do I make particles?
Create smoke or sparks
Play an effect when an enemy dies
Why are my particles huge?
prerequisites: A scene is open and the intended effect location is known
steps: Create a Particle System and position it at the effect origin.
Tune Start Lifetime, Start Speed, Start Size, and the Shape module at a low emission rate.
Use Color over Lifetime and Size over Lifetime to make particles fade naturally.
Disable Play On Awake if a script should call Play at a specific event.
verification: Preview or trigger the effect and confirm its scale, direction, duration, and looping match the intended event.
common_mistakes: Using excessive emission and hiding the scene.
Ignoring Simulation Space when the emitter moves.
Leaving a one-shot effect looping forever.

title: Add basic post-processing
summary: Use a global volume and pipeline-compatible overrides to adjust exposure, color, bloom, and other screen effects.
example_questions: How do I add bloom?
Use post-processing in URP
Add color grading
Why does my Volume have no effect?
prerequisites: The project render pipeline and active gameplay camera are known
steps: Create a global Volume and create or assign a Volume Profile.
Add one override such as Bloom, Color Adjustments, or Tonemapping.
Enable post-processing on the active camera or pipeline configuration where required.
Tune modest values while comparing the Game view with the override enabled and disabled.
verification: The Game view visibly changes when the Volume is enabled and returns to the original appearance when disabled.
common_mistakes: Following instructions for a different render pipeline.
Forgetting the camera post-processing toggle.
Using extreme bloom or exposure to hide lighting problems.

title: Save a simple setting with PlayerPrefs
summary: Store small primitive preferences such as volume or a best score and load them with safe defaults.
example_questions: How do I save volume settings?
Remember a high score
What is PlayerPrefs?
Load a saved value when the game starts
prerequisites: A small int, float, or string value needs to persist
steps: Choose one stable key name and a sensible default value.
Load with PlayerPrefs.GetInt, GetFloat, or GetString during initialization.
Write the value only when it changes using the matching Set method.
Call PlayerPrefs.Save at an appropriate checkpoint if immediate persistence is important.
verification: Change the setting, stop and restart the game, and confirm the value is restored.
common_mistakes: Using PlayerPrefs for large, structured, or security-sensitive save data.
Using different key spelling when saving and loading.
Writing every frame.

title: Keep a manager across scene loads
summary: Use DontDestroyOnLoad carefully for one long-lived manager and prevent duplicate instances.
example_questions: How do I keep music between scenes?
Use DontDestroyOnLoad
Why do managers duplicate after changing scenes?
Keep game state during scene transitions
prerequisites: A manager or music object should outlive one scene
steps: Place the long-lived behavior on a root GameObject.
In Awake, check whether another instance already exists and destroy the duplicate if it does.
Store the accepted instance and call DontDestroyOnLoad on its GameObject.
Remove copies from later scenes and reconnect scene-specific references after each load when needed.
verification: Move through several scenes and confirm exactly one manager remains and its intended state persists.
common_mistakes: Calling DontDestroyOnLoad on a child object.
Keeping duplicate managers from every scene.
Holding destroyed references to objects from the previous scene.

title: Reuse frequently spawned objects with a pool

prerequisites: The game repeatedly creates and removes the same prefab type
steps: Confirm with the Profiler that repeated spawning is worth optimizing.
Create a pool with a function that instantiates the prefab and functions that activate and deactivate instances.
Reset position, rotation, velocity, timers, and other state whenever an instance is taken from the pool.
Return the object to the pool instead of destroying it when its job is complete.
verification: Repeated use reactivates existing instance IDs and every reused object starts in a clean state.
